proposals.rationale: R22 proposes an advance notice and voluntary demonstration, while R31 recommends using out-of-range experimental populations only as a last resort.

proposals.name: Affected-Population Coverage
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment identifies relevant affected groups and explains why the proposal must account for their differing circumstances; score 0 when it invokes a population broadly without analyzing who is affected or how.
proposals.rationale: R08 explains why driver research should cover ages beyond 25–54, and R10 examines low-internet-access, rural, older, lower-income, and bilingual populations.

proposals.name: Evaluation Design
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment specifies how effectiveness, validity, accuracy, compliance, or unintended effects could be measured; score 0 when it makes claims without describing any way to test them.
proposals.rationale: R09 describes a reproducible estimation method for underride crashes, while R59 discusses validity, reliability, construct representation, and empirical testing of assessment items.

proposals.name: Time-Horizon Reasoning
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment distinguishes immediate effects from longer-term consequences, feedback, recovery, or intergenerational impacts; score 0 when it discusses only a single undifferentiated time point.
proposals.rationale: R02 separates immediate fishing restrictions from cultural and livelihood consequences, while R23 contrasts short-term user benefits with long-term fishery recovery.

proposals.name: Merits Beyond Procedure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a procedural request also supplies substantive analysis of the underlying proposal; score 0 when the comment consists solely of requesting more time, acknowledging receipt, or providing administrative information.
proposals.rationale: R11, R20, R40, and R58 primarily request comment-period extensions, illustrating the distinction between procedural participation and substantive policy analysis.

proposals.name: Information Gain
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment contributes new facts, analysis, examples, or implications beyond stating a position; score 0 when it merely expresses support, opposition, concurrence, or preference without adding usable substance.
proposals.rationale: R17 says it concurs with no additional comments, R55 simply supports adjusting fees, and R42 offers general support without policy-specific analysis.

proposals.name: Qualified And Balanced Reasoning
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the comment acknowledges uncertainty, competing considerations, limits, or conditions and still reaches a reasoned position; score 0 when it relies on absolute assertions, internal contradictions, or unqualified rhetoric.
proposals.rationale: R31 supports the proposal while retaining native-ecosystem safeguards, whereas R13 combines strong claims with uncertainty and extended tangential discussion.

proposals.name: Institutional status cues
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text explicitly signals institutional office, executive or professional title, organizational scale, credentials, or official capacity; do not judge whether any signal is good, relevant, or deserved.
proposals.rationale: Senior or well-resourced institutions may receive systematic text-processing advantages, while also having more capacity to produce genuinely substantive comments. This fingerprint appears in the official titles and institutional descriptions in R01 and R04.

proposals.name: Professional drafting signals
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text shows visible signs of lawyer, regulatory-affairs, or technical drafting assistance, such as named counsel, formal legal structure, dense sectioning, or document-control conventions; do not judge whether the drafting is good or accurate.
proposals.rationale: Professional assistance can create recognizable textual polish that is predictive for a text-only system, and it may also improve genuine substantive work. The pattern is visible in R40 and R53.

proposals.name: Submission artifact markers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text contains transmission or ingestion artifacts such as attachment placeholders, email headers, fax details, file names, upload notices, or archived-message metadata; do not judge whether these artifacts help or hurt the comment.
proposals.rationale: Different submission channels and docket-ingestion routines can leave machine-readable traces unrelated to argument content. Examples include R02 and R19.

proposals.name: Coalition breadth
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text names multiple joint commenters, member organizations, represented constituencies, or broad organizational networks; do not judge whether the coalition is representative, important, or persuasive.
proposals.rationale: Networked organizations can generate distinctive group-signaling language and may also pool expertise that improves substantive work. This fingerprint is evident in R16 and R58.

proposals.name: Experiential proximity
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text presents the author as personally or occupationally embedded in the affected activity, location, industry, or population; do not judge whether that experience makes the claims good, credible, or relevant.
proposals.rationale: Direct experience leaves first-person role and exposure markers that can influence text-based interpretation, while sometimes contributing genuinely useful information. Examples are R13 and R60.
proposals.upstream_parent: author access to lived or occupational experience

proposals.name: Timing and process references
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text explicitly mentions deadlines, extensions, prior versions, delayed responses, reopened periods, meetings, or holiday timing; do not judge whether the timing is appropriate or useful.
proposals.rationale: Production and submission timing can leave visible procedural references that act as nuisance signals without changing the substantive content. The pattern appears in R10 and R22.

proposals.name: Procedural boilerplate
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text uses stock procedural language such as courtesy acknowledgments, extension requests, concurrence statements, or declarations that no further comments will be offered; do not judge whether the boilerplate is appropriate or effective.
proposals.rationale: Comment genre and institutional templates can be predictive stylistic markers independent of substance. Examples include R06 and R51.

proposals.name: Quantitative density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text contains explicit numbers, measurements, percentages, dollar amounts, sample sizes, dates, footnotes, or formal source references; do not judge the accuracy, relevance, or importance of those details.
proposals.rationale: Analytical resources may produce conspicuous numerical detail that a text system treats as a signal, while also enabling better substantive analysis. This fingerprint is visible in R10 and R42.

proposals.name: Affective rhetoric
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text uses emotionally charged, urgent, moralizing, adversarial, celebratory, or personal-value language, including direct appeals and emphatic phrasing; do not judge whether the rhetoric is persuasive or appropriate.
proposals.rationale: Rhetorical intensity is a detectable style feature that can affect text processing without establishing substantive quality. Examples include R19 and R52.

proposals.name: OCR and layout irregularity
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text shows OCR-like substitutions, broken words, typographical errors, malformed punctuation, inconsistent spacing, or visibly degraded layout; do not judge whether the errors affect meaning or quality.
proposals.rationale: Scanning, OCR, and archival conversion can create nuisance signals unrelated to the underlying comment. The artifacts are apparent in R02 and R05.
